Karoo Uranium II

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
Plans to mine uranium and molybdenum through open cast mining in the Karoo are still on the cards, with organisations fighting tooth and nail against it. The mining company's applications for mining rights in 3 blocks between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen are still pending, as are its applications to prospect in five more areas.

A draft Environmental Impact Assessment report for one of the planned mining areas gives us a more accurate idea of how the mining company plans to mitigate the possible negative effects - and opponents are unimpressed. The mining company has no plans to preserve any of the normal vegetation but says it will remove and preserve the threatened plants, to be replanted during mine rehabilitation. It says it will educate mine workers not to kill the animals that live in the area. The area has high paleontological value but, since it is difficult to do any digging in the area, the mining may even make it easier for paleontologists to explore the area, the report states. It also says any radiation that people may be exposed to will be minimal.

Philip McNaughton farms in the Kareepoort area, which is subject to a mining right application. Earlier this year, he discovered a tiny flowering succulent he had never seen before. Experts say that this is possibly a new species, and it may be under threat from the planned mining.

Meanwhile, the Council for Geoscience also has plans to conduct a 3-year study that will involve the drilling of deep research boreholes near Beaufort-West to assess the effect that mining and exploration activities in the area could have and has on the deep & shallow ground water, seismicity, soil chemistry and gas emission. The planned uranium mining and fracking are often criticised because adequate data and analysis of the possible impacts are not available and the Council for Geoscience's research would address this.

Summary:
Carte Blanche first reported on plans to mine uranium and molybdenum in the Karoo in August last year. Nearly 10 months later, Tasman RSA Mines is pushing ahead with its application for mining rights in three areas between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen. The company also has pending prospecting rights applications for another five areas.

Quaggasfontein, just outside Beaufort-West, is one of the areas subject to a mining rights application. This is where a borehole was planned to supply water for the town. Tasman RSA Mines admitted to us last year that there are concerns about this area and that they would have to make a plan to mitigate possible effects on water sources here - but no Environmental Impact Assessment is available for this area yet.

The public had time until last month to comment on the draft Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for the mining in one of the areas - Kareepoort, about 60km east of Beaufort-West and 50 km west of Aberdeen. The draft EIA acknowledges that the area is a unique and sensitive habitat and home to a number of threatened and near-threatened animal and plant species. It also has a unique character and paleontological value. But any potential damage to the environment and character can be mitigated, the draft report says.

The report also says the potential economic advantages for the area are great - this while the report states that only 16 permanent positions will be created in the mining operations here.

One of the main criticisms raised by organisations opposing the mining is that the EIA only assesses the impact on this one area and does not take the cumulative effects into account.

Further information:
What locals believed to be a victory last year when Tasman RSA Mines drastically shrunk the areas it wanted to mine, has proven to be quite the opposite. There are serious concerns about the sensitivity of the areas still targeted.

The company admitted to us last year that there were concerns about Quaggasfontein, one of the areas it has applied to mine. The concerns are related to the water sources here. Quaggasfontein is where one of the additional boreholes were planned to supply water to the town of Beaufort-West. Tasman told us it would have to make a plan to mitigate possible effects here - but there is no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for this area as of yet.

The draft EIA for another area the company wants to mine, Kareepoort, acknowledges that the area is a unique and sensitive habitat and home to a number of threatened and near-threatened animal and plant species, as well as an area with a unique character and high paleontological value. But any potential damage to the environment and character can be mitigated with measures like dust suppression, removal and storage of sensitive plants to be replanted after mining is finished and careful rehabilitation, the draft report says.

Local farmer Philip McNaughton fears that mining could mean the end to a tiny succulent, thought to be a new species, that he discovered in the potential mining area this year.

According to the draft EIA, the area is mostly used for sheep grazing and only a few people would have to be relocated. Any possible exposure to radiation for locals (due to the radioactive nature of uranium) is minimal, it says.

The report also says the potential economic advantages for the area are great - but the figures on job creation has one questioning whether this is accurate.

The final report is expected by 31 July, while the EIAs for the 2 other areas are still being awaited.

Tasman RSA Mines plan to conduct open cast mining at Kareepoort, and then transport the ore 20 km by road to the processing plant planned for Rystkuil, another of the three mining areas, just southwest of Beaufort-West.

One of the main criticisms raised by organisations opposing the mining is that the EIA only assesses the impact on this one area and does not take the cumulative effects into account.

The South African Faith Communities' Environmental Initiative (one of the parties who won the court victory against the country's nuclear plans) as well as Agri Eastern Cape and Agri Western Cape have submitted responses to the draft EIA. They are all of the opinion that the EIA was not comprehensive enough. The study was clearly conducted over too short a period and many potential effects were watered down, they claim.

On at least one front, the Council for Geoscience has plans to address the lack of adequate data and information that is cited in the battle against uranium mining and fracking in the Karoo. The Council plans to conduct a 3-year study that will involve the drilling of deep research boreholes near Beaufort-West to assess the effect that mining and exploration activities in the area could have and has on the deep & shallow ground water, seismicity, soil chemistry and gas emission.


Extra Budget Items:
Filming may need to be extended to three days, as the distances will necessitate two days for filming in the Karoo. But we also have to do 2 interviews in Pretoria: with Tim van Stormbroek of Ferret Mining & Environmental Solutions, which compiled the draft EIA, and Dr Luc Chevallier of the Council for Geoscience.

Press Release:


Uranium in the Karoo
The future of the Karoo hangs in the balance as plans to mine rich uranium deposits through open cast mining inch forward. Residents and organisations have been fighting
it tooth and nail, saying it would pollute what little water this arid area has for farming and domestic use. But a possible new plant species has also been discovered in the
proposed mining area and may just halt the entire process. Carte Blanche heads back to Beaufort West for an update on the progress of the mining application.

Script:


KAROO URANIUM 2 SCRIPT
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: John Webb
TX: TBC

The Central Karoo is set to change forever if Australian-owned Tasman RSA Mines gets the right to mine uranium in the area -- a plan they pitched to the people of Beaufort West last year -- people hungry for jobs and contracts.

(STRAP: Carte Blanche August 2016) UPS: JOHN WEBB: 250 permanent jobs isn’t going to solve the unemployment crisis in the Karoo, let’s be frank.

TEFO MALOISANE, DIRECTOR, TASMAN RSA MINES: I have yet to meet a business in Beaufort-West that employs 250 people.
The uranium has always been there, but when it’s extracted and processed, it can release toxic heavy metals and gases like radon, which has been linked to lung cancer in mine workers elsewhere. Should the soil or water be contaminated, the effects will be hard to fix.

(STRAP: Carte Blanche August 2016) DR STEFAN CRAMER, HYDROGEOLOGIST: We’ll see a Karoo devastated by open pit and unrehabilitated mine sites.

Tasman wants to dig open pits of up to 60 metres deep. The company hired Ferret Mining and Environmental Services to assess the impact mining might have. Tim van Stormbroek leads the team.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: It’s our job to give the applicant a hard time.
The Environmental Impact Assessment or EIA analyses the potential damage to the environment and people. It details the steps Tasman must take to limit the impact. Based on this, government must decide to grant a mining right … or not.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: If this document is approved by the Department of Mineral Resources, it becomes legally binding. And so, the client is obligated to commit and implement everything that is...

JOHN WEBB: But as you say, obligated inasmuch as they have to prove to a department that they’re doing the right thing and the department needs to police that.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: Yes, yes.

Mining will happen at Kareepoort, Quaggasfontein and Rystkuil, where uranium was mined in the seventies - it’s earmarked for Tasman’s central processing plant.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: This uranium project sits on the back of historical uranium prospecting and trial mining in the area… There’s been years and years of…continual monitoring.

JOHN LINK: This process has been moving apace with those opposed to the mining application often struggling to keep up -- so who would have thought that a tiny succulent plant no bigger than a R5 coin would bring everything to a screeching halt?

The draft EIA for Kareepoort was out for public comment until mid-April, while the drafts for the other two areas were due by the end of May, but the deadlines were pushed back by several months thanks to the discovery of this potentially new plant species at Kareepoort.

PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: This is probably the most visible you’re ever going to find them, they’re green, they’re growing.

The McNaughtons’ farm borders Kareepoort. Phillip and Joan believe in low-impact farming to allow the veld time to recover. They were checking on their grazing when Joan spotted this unfamiliar succulent.

PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: It was such a unique tiny little plant hidden in silty cracks and you know, we’ve been here for 20 years and we probably walked on it. That’s the nature of the Karoo. You never quite know what you’re going to find next.

It had to be the right kind of rainy season for this Nananthus to poke its spiky head and bright yellow flower through the clay. Joan posted pictures on the South African Botanical Institute’s iSPOT website and within hours experts from around the world confirmed this could be a new species. Tasman had to go back to the drawing board.

JOHN WEBB: How did your client respond to the delay? Bloody plant?

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: No. Was very happy to…we had to motivate the reasons behind it and the motivation was very strong. The client then proceeded with the application to the DMR for the extension. If that species turns out to be a species that is only found in that area and not in a wider area, we have a significant red flag.

Back in the Karoo this year, we found that people were more informed -- and far more concerned -- about uranium mining. More than a thousand people have commented on the EIA.

JOHN LINK: We’re close to a year down the line and while there’s a lot more information on what this mining operation will eventually look like...those in support of the application and those opposed to it, are as far apart as they’ve ever been.
Geologist Jan Arkert studied the report on behalf of the Southern African Faith Communities’ Environment Initiative -- the organisation that, together with Earthlife Africa, successfully challenged the government on its nuclear purchasing process earlier this year.

JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: We’ve got local and international experts looking at it on our behalf and we’ve had some significant reservations about it. Some basically stating that this… the report is not actually worth it and that they should begin again.

PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: We’ve put over 240 species of plants on iSpot and this is within 30 kilometres of where they did their assessments, they only positively identified 55...even from an amateur point of view you can question why is there this difference.

Ferret’s draft EIA notes that various threatened plants, animals and birds are found in the target area. It recommends keeping a seed bank, relocating sensitive plants, and instructing mine workers not to kill any animals. But where is the bigger picture, critics want to know, when three separate EIAs are being done for the three blocks and Tasman also has a further five pending prospecting applications.

JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: You cannot look at that particular isolated little block without looking at what’s proposed in the future.

JOHN WEBB: Are you referring to what is called the cumulative approach?

JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: Precisely, John. I mean, I… my analogy to this situation now is a little bit like watching a rugby game looking through a keyhole. You can see what’s directly in front of you but you don’t see what’s happening on the sides of the field.

Environmental lawyer Walter Anderson prepared Agri Western Cape’s submission on the draft EIA.

WALTER ANDERSON, ENVIRONMENTAL LAWYER FOR AGRI WESTERN CAPE: We think it’s highly problematic that the impact assessment of these three projects have been fragmented, because it’s now not possible for the cumulative assessment to take place.

But Van Stormbroek says they’re just following government orders.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: I agree that the cumulative impact is vitally important. We had that conversation with the competent authority at the start of the piece to say can we not put this all together in one basket. It was the desire of the client to do so. But from a legislative perspective they’ve said no.

JOHN LINK: In many ways this debate is about the tug of war between the environment and the potential cash injection into some of the Karoo’s poorest communities. The question is do we have the correct information that’ll enable us to make an informed decision, one way or the other.

Interested and affected people will have another chance to comment when Ferret releases the new EIAs. Chris Hayward is mobilising fellow farmers to keep uranium mining out.

CHRIS HAYWARD, ACTIVIST, STOP URANIUM MINING IN THE KAROO: We do not want poison in our environment...my water level drops and I don’t have water, my sheep have to go. And if my sheep have to go, I have to go. And I have to go, my staff have to go. in the EIA they deliberately have applied for a licence to work in the Kareepoort block for 4 and a half years. My question is, what happens 4 years 7 months later. We are left with a pile of rubble. We’re left with toxins and who’s going to monitor all these piles of rubble?

WALTER ANDERSON, ENVIRONMENTAL LAWYER FOR AGRI WESTERN CAPE: The Karoo is particularly vulnerable...not even to speak about what would happen if proprietary marks like Karoo lamb was affected by the market’s perception that there might be radioactive accumulation in the wool or in the meat and we don’t think that the applicants addressed this.
Chairman of the Greater Karoo Community Policing Forum Mohamed Adams fears the upheaval of a short-lived mining boom.

MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: If the industry upon whose back the economy is going to be grown for the next hundred years, is going to leave a desolation for ages to come, then it certainly it’s something that we cannot support. My challenge to anyone trying to engage in uranium mining if you’re willing to work the mine yourself, if you’re willing to buy a property in Beaufort West and move here with your family and live here for the foreseeable future, then I will be willing to consider doing the same. But as long as you are completely removed from the situation and the dangers that it poses, I don’t feel you have a right to dictate to us what we do with the wealth and riches of the Karoo.

JOHN WEBB: If this mine or these mines go ahead and the mitigation doesn’t happen the way you hope -- or even if it does and yet the groundwater still becomes contaminated...and the radioactive particles travel a lot further than was anticipated, people become sick...would you be happy to have your name associated with that report that effectively smoothed the way?

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: If what you describe becomes a reality, you have my commitment that I’ll go back to the people of Beaufort West and have a look at the issues that that have presented themselves. Monitoring processes give you early warning of issues that are perhaps not happening exactly as they were modelled to happen.

MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: I don’t think it’s about finding a way to make uranium safe and palatable. The dialogue should be about finding an alternative to uranium to begin with. If we consider the water crisis currently facing this province and this country, then I believe water and fresh water is going to be a more valuable commodity in the next 50 years than any lump of uranium is ever going to be.

PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: Farming sustainably we can produce foreign exchange and jobs forever. The only thing they can do forever is contaminate this area.

CHRIS HAYWARD, ACTIVIST, STOP URANIUM MINING IN THE KAROO: Uranium, we feel, is best left where mother nature has kept it close to her bosom all these millions of years.


PROMOS

The face of the Karoo may change forever if plans to mine uranium there gets the green light. But many locals are fighting hard to keep the miners out.

15 secs:
Plans to mine uranium in the Karoo hit a snag -- as local farmers discover what experts say could be a unique, new species in the proposed mining area.
PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON: That’s the nature of the Karoo. You never quite know what you’re going to find next.

15 secs:
Opposition to uranium mining in the Karoo mounts as the environmental reports are scrutinised...
MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: I believe water and fresh water is going to be a more valuable commodity in the next 50 years than any lump of uranium is ever going to be.

TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: If this document is approved by the Department of Mineral Resources, it becomes legally binding. And so, the client is obligated to commit and implement everything that is... JOHN WEBB: But as you say, obligated inasmuch as they have to prove to a department that they’re doing the right thing and the department needs to police that. TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: Yes, yes. Mining will happen at Kareepoort, Quaggasfontein and Rystkuil, where uranium was mined in the seventies - it’s earmarked for Tasman’s central processing plant. TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: This uranium project sits on the back of historical uranium prospecting and trial mining in the area… There’s been years and years of…continual monitoring. JOHN LINK: This process has been moving apace with those opposed to the mining application often struggling to keep up -- so who would have thought that a tiny succulent plant no bigger than a R5 coin would bring everything to a screeching halt? The draft EIA for Kareepoort was out for public comment until mid-April, while the drafts for the other two areas were due by the end of May, but the deadlines were pushed back by several months thanks to the discovery of this potentially new plant species at Kareepoort. PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: This is probably the most visible you’re ever going to find them, they’re green, they’re growing. The McNaughtons’ farm borders Kareepoort. Phillip and Joan believe in low-impact farming to allow the veld time to recover. They were checking on their grazing when Joan spotted this unfamiliar succulent. PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: It was such a unique tiny little plant hidden in silty cracks and you know, we’ve been here for 20 years and we probably walked on it. That’s the nature of the Karoo. You never quite know what you’re going to find next. It had to be the right kind of rainy season for this Nananthus to poke its spiky head and bright yellow flower through the clay. Joan posted pictures on the South African Botanical Institute’s iSPOT website and within hours experts from around the world confirmed this could be a new species. Tasman had to go back to the drawing board. JOHN WEBB: How did your client respond to the delay? Bloody plant? TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: No. Was very happy to…we had to motivate the reasons behind it and the motivation was very strong. The client then proceeded with the application to the DMR for the extension. If that species turns out to be a species that is only found in that area and not in a wider area, we have a significant red flag. Back in the Karoo this year, we found that people were more informed -- and far more concerned -- about uranium mining. More than a thousand people have commented on the EIA. JOHN LINK: We’re close to a year down the line and while there’s a lot more information on what this mining operation will eventually look like...those in support of the application and those opposed to it, are as far apart as they’ve ever been. Geologist Jan Arkert studied the report on behalf of the Southern African Faith Communities’ Environment Initiative -- the organisation that, together with Earthlife Africa, successfully challenged the government on its nuclear purchasing process earlier this year. JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: We’ve got local and international experts looking at it on our behalf and we’ve had some significant reservations about it. Some basically stating that this… the report is not actually worth it and that they should begin again. PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: We’ve put over 240 species of plants on iSpot and this is within 30 kilometres of where they did their assessments, they only positively identified 55...even from an amateur point of view you can question why is there this difference. Ferret’s draft EIA notes that various threatened plants, animals and birds are found in the target area. It recommends keeping a seed bank, relocating sensitive plants, and instructing mine workers not to kill any animals. But where is the bigger picture, critics want to know, when three separate EIAs are being done for the three blocks and Tasman also has a further five pending prospecting applications. JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: You cannot look at that particular isolated little block without looking at what’s proposed in the future. JOHN WEBB: Are you referring to what is called the cumulative approach? JAN ARKERT, GEOLOGIST: Precisely, John. I mean, I… my analogy to this situation now is a little bit like watching a rugby game looking through a keyhole. You can see what’s directly in front of you but you don’t see what’s happening on the sides of the field. Environmental lawyer Walter Anderson prepared Agri Western Cape’s submission on the draft EIA. WALTER ANDERSON, ENVIRONMENTAL LAWYER FOR AGRI WESTERN CAPE: We think it’s highly problematic that the impact assessment of these three projects have been fragmented, because it’s now not possible for the cumulative assessment to take place. But Van Stormbroek says they’re just following government orders. TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: I agree that the cumulative impact is vitally important. We had that conversation with the competent authority at the start of the piece to say can we not put this all together in one basket. It was the desire of the client to do so. But from a legislative perspective they’ve said no. JOHN LINK: In many ways this debate is about the tug of war between the environment and the potential cash injection into some of the Karoo’s poorest communities. The question is do we have the correct information that’ll enable us to make an informed decision, one way or the other. Interested and affected people will have another chance to comment when Ferret releases the new EIAs. Chris Hayward is mobilising fellow farmers to keep uranium mining out. CHRIS HAYWARD, ACTIVIST, STOP URANIUM MINING IN THE KAROO: We do not want poison in our environment...my water level drops and I don’t have water, my sheep have to go. And if my sheep have to go, I have to go. And I have to go, my staff have to go. in the EIA they deliberately have applied for a licence to work in the Kareepoort block for 4 and a half years. My question is, what happens 4 years 7 months later. We are left with a pile of rubble. We’re left with toxins and who’s going to monitor all these piles of rubble? WALTER ANDERSON, ENVIRONMENTAL LAWYER FOR AGRI WESTERN CAPE: The Karoo is particularly vulnerable...not even to speak about what would happen if proprietary marks like Karoo lamb was affected by the market’s perception that there might be radioactive accumulation in the wool or in the meat and we don’t think that the applicants addressed this. Chairman of the Greater Karoo Community Policing Forum Mohamed Adams fears the upheaval of a short-lived mining boom. MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: If the industry upon whose back the economy is going to be grown for the next hundred years, is going to leave a desolation for ages to come, then it certainly it’s something that we cannot support. My challenge to anyone trying to engage in uranium mining if you’re willing to work the mine yourself, if you’re willing to buy a property in Beaufort West and move here with your family and live here for the foreseeable future, then I will be willing to consider doing the same. But as long as you are completely removed from the situation and the dangers that it poses, I don’t feel you have a right to dictate to us what we do with the wealth and riches of the Karoo. JOHN WEBB: If this mine or these mines go ahead and the mitigation doesn’t happen the way you hope -- or even if it does and yet the groundwater still becomes contaminated...and the radioactive particles travel a lot further than was anticipated, people become sick...would you be happy to have your name associated with that report that effectively smoothed the way? TIM VAN STORMBROEK, FERRET MINING AND ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES: If what you describe becomes a reality, you have my commitment that I’ll go back to the people of Beaufort West and have a look at the issues that that have presented themselves. Monitoring processes give you early warning of issues that are perhaps not happening exactly as they were modelled to happen. MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: I don’t think it’s about finding a way to make uranium safe and palatable. The dialogue should be about finding an alternative to uranium to begin with. If we consider the water crisis currently facing this province and this country, then I believe water and fresh water is going to be a more valuable commodity in the next 50 years than any lump of uranium is ever going to be. PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON, FARMER: Farming sustainably we can produce foreign exchange and jobs forever. The only thing they can do forever is contaminate this area. CHRIS HAYWARD, ACTIVIST, STOP URANIUM MINING IN THE KAROO: Uranium, we feel, is best left where mother nature has kept it close to her bosom all these millions of years. PROMOS 10 secs: The face of the Karoo may change forever if plans to mine uranium there gets the green light. But many locals are fighting hard to keep the miners out. 15 secs: Plans to mine uranium in the Karoo hit a snag -- as local farmers discover what experts say could be a unique, new species in the proposed mining area. PHILLIP MCNAUGHTON: That’s the nature of the Karoo. You never quite know what you’re going to find next. 15 secs: Opposition to uranium mining in the Karoo mounts as the environmental reports are scrutinised... MOHAMED ADAMS, CHAIRMAN, GREATER KAROO CPF: I believe water and fresh water is going to be a more valuable commodity in the next 50 years than any lump of uranium is ever going to be.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Plans to mine uranium and molybdenum through open cast mining in the Karoo are still on the cards, with organisations fighting tooth and nail against it. The mining company's applications for mining rights in 3 blocks between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen are still pending, as are its applications to prospect in five more areas. A draft Environmental Impact Assessment report for one of the planned mining areas gives us a more accurate idea of how the mining company plans to mitigate the possible negative effects - and opponents are unimpressed. The mining company has no plans to preserve any of the normal vegetation but says it will remove and preserve the threatened plants, to be replanted during mine rehabilitation. It says it will educate mine workers not to kill the animals that live in the area. The area has high paleontological value but, since it is difficult to do any digging in the area, the mining may even make it easier for paleontologists to explore the area, the report states. It also says any radiation that people may be exposed to will be minimal. Philip McNaughton farms in the Kareepoort area, which is subject to a mining right application. Earlier this year, he discovered a tiny flowering succulent he had never seen before. Experts say that this is possibly a new species, and it may be under threat from the planned mining. Meanwhile, the Council for Geoscience also has plans to conduct a 3-year study that will involve the drilling of deep research boreholes near Beaufort-West to assess the effect that mining and exploration activities in the area could have and has on the deep & shallow ground water, seismicity, soil chemistry and gas emission. The planned uranium mining and fracking are often criticised because adequate data and analysis of the possible impacts are not available and the Council for Geoscience's research would address this.
metadata.Summary: Carte Blanche first reported on plans to mine uranium and molybdenum in the Karoo in August last year. Nearly 10 months later, Tasman RSA Mines is pushing ahead with its application for mining rights in three areas between Beaufort-West and Aberdeen. The company also has pending prospecting rights applications for another five areas. Quaggasfontein, just outside Beaufort-West, is one of the areas subject to a mining rights application. This is where a borehole was planned to supply water for the town. Tasman RSA Mines admitted to us last year that there are concerns about this area and that they would have to make a plan to mitigate possible effects on water sources here - but no Environmental Impact Assessment is available for this area yet. The public had time until last month to comment on the draft Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for the mining in one of the areas - Kareepoort, about 60km east of Beaufort-West and 50 km west of Aberdeen. The draft EIA acknowledges that the area is a unique and sensitive habitat and home to a number of threatened and near-threatened animal and plant species. It also has a unique character and paleontological value. But any potential damage to the environment and character can be mitigated, the draft report says. The report also says the potential economic advantages for the area are great - this while the report states that only 16 permanent positions will be created in the mining operations here. One of the main criticisms raised by organisations opposing the mining is that the EIA only assesses the impact on this one area and does not take the cumulative effects into account.
metadata.Further information: What locals believed to be a victory last year when Tasman RSA Mines drastically shrunk the areas it wanted to mine, has proven to be quite the opposite. There are serious concerns about the sensitivity of the areas still targeted. The company admitted to us last year that there were concerns about Quaggasfontein, one of the areas it has applied to mine. The concerns are related to the water sources here. Quaggasfontein is where one of the additional boreholes were planned to supply water to the town of Beaufort-West. Tasman told us it would have to make a plan to mitigate possible effects here - but there is no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for this area as of yet. The draft EIA for another area the company wants to mine, Kareepoort, acknowledges that the area is a unique and sensitive habitat and home to a number of threatened and near-threatened animal and plant species, as well as an area with a unique character and high paleontological value. But any potential damage to the environment and character can be mitigated with measures like dust suppression, removal and storage of sensitive plants to be replanted after mining is finished and careful rehabilitation, the draft report says. Local farmer Philip McNaughton fears that mining could mean the end to a tiny succulent, thought to be a new species, that he discovered in the potential mining area this year. According to the draft EIA, the area is mostly used for sheep grazing and only a few people would have to be relocated. Any possible exposure to radiation for locals (due to the radioactive nature of uranium) is minimal, it says. The report also says the potential economic advantages for the area are great - but the figures on job creation has one questioning whether this is accurate. The final report is expected by 31 July, while the EIAs for the 2 other areas are still being awaited. Tasman RSA Mines plan to conduct open cast mining at Kareepoort, and then transport the ore 20 km by road to the processing plant planned for Rystkuil, another of the three mining areas, just southwest of Beaufort-West. One of the main criticisms raised by organisations opposing the mining is that the EIA only assesses the impact on this one area and does not take the cumulative effects into account. The South African Faith Communities' Environmental Initiative (one of the parties who won the court victory against the country's nuclear plans) as well as Agri Eastern Cape and Agri Western Cape have submitted responses to the draft EIA. They are all of the opinion that the EIA was not comprehensive enough. The study was clearly conducted over too short a period and many potential effects were watered down, they claim. On at least one front, the Council for Geoscience has plans to address the lack of adequate data and information that is cited in the battle against uranium mining and fracking in the Karoo. The Council plans to conduct a 3-year study that will involve the drilling of deep research boreholes near Beaufort-West to assess the effect that mining and exploration activities in the area could have and has on the deep & shallow ground water, seismicity, soil chemistry and gas emission.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: Filming may need to be extended to three days, as the distances will necessitate two days for filming in the Karoo. But we also have to do 2 interviews in Pretoria: with Tim van Stormbroek of Ferret Mining & Environmental Solutions, which compiled the draft EIA, and Dr Luc Chevallier of the Council for Geoscience.
